# Shorted Battery on 2020 Mercedes A35, Now Car Won't Start

A high-voltage arc inside an engine bay is rarely a clean event. When a piece of metal casing on the ECU housing contacts the positive battery terminal, the resulting short circuit doesn't just melt a wire; it injects massive current into the vehicle's ground and power distribution networks. In your 2020 Mercedes A35 AMG case, the symptoms you are seeingâaccessory mode functioning but zero ignition outputâare classic indicators of a system that has entered a protective lockout state or suffered a catastrophic ground fault that bypassed standard fuse protection.

You correctly identified that the accessory power is present. The fact that the dash displays and radio screen light up confirms that the low-voltage domain (12V) and specific communication buses are intact. However, the starter solenoid and ignition coils require a dedicated high-current path that was severed during the arc. When you tested continuity on the battery terminals, finding the green line points good but the red line point open is a critical clue. The "green line" likely represents the pyrotechnic fuse (pyro fuse) which protects the main starter circuit, while the "red line" likely indicates the charge sensor or a specific pre-fuse link that failed to carry current.

The immediate assumption that a simple fuse blew in the charge sensor is understandable but technically risky without verifying the nature of the failure. Fuses are designed to open only once when the current exceeds their rating. If you tested continuity on the main pre-fuses (125A and 80A) and they read "OK," you must verify if these readings represent a continuous circuit or an open circuit where the multimeter is measuring infinite resistance across a broken fuse link. A standard digital multimeter in continuity mode will beep for a closed loop but remain silent for an open one; ensure you aren't misinterpreting the lack of a beep as a "good" connection rather than a blown component.

The bypass attempt using jumper cables from the positive terminal to the end of the pyro fuse is a valid diagnostic step, yet its failure suggests the issue isn't just a missing link in the starter circuit. If the jumper provides no power to the starter solenoid, the fault likely lies upstream in the main bus or within the Battery Management System (BMS). Modern Mercedes-Benz models with integrated start/stop systems often include a high-current fuse and a charge sensor directly at the battery. If the arc caused damage to the BMS logic board or if the charge sensor itself is internally shorted, the vehicle's software may be disabling the starter output as a safety measure to prevent further battery depletion or fire risk.

There is also the possibility of a "soft" short where the metal casing didn't just touch the terminal but bridged other sensitive components. The ECU housing arc could have damaged the wiring harness behind it, causing an intermittent high-resistance connection that your continuity tester isn't catching under load. To diagnose this, you need to perform a voltage drop test across the main battery cables while attempting to crank the engine. If you see more than 0.5V drop across the positive cable or ground strap during cranking, you have found your culprit: high resistance in the path due to melted insulation or corroded contacts from the arc.

If the BMS is indeed disabled by the short, simply replacing fuses won't restore function; the system may require a battery registration reset or a diagnostic scan via the STAR Diagnosis system to clear the "short circuit" fault code stored in the memory. In many cases, a severe arc event compromises the integrity of the battery cells themselves, leading to an internal short that prevents the battery from sustaining the high discharge rate required for starter engagement. Before replacing expensive components, verify the state of health (SOH) of the battery by measuring its open-circuit voltage after it has rested for several hours and checking for any signs of thermal damage or bulging on the casing.
